title: Finding Beauty in Decay
subtitle: Why imperfection is the heart of fine art photography
excerpt: The most compelling images often emerge from the least perfect subjects. A reflection on why I'm drawn to textures, erosion, and the marks that time leaves behind.
content:
There's a Japanese concept called wabi-sabi — the acceptance and appreciation of imperfection, impermanence, and incompleteness. It's a philosophy that has profoundly shaped the way I approach my work.

When I walk through an abandoned building or trace my fingers along a weathered wall, I'm not seeing decay. I'm seeing a story written in texture. Every crack, every layer of peeling paint, every rust stain is a chapter in a narrative that spans decades, sometimes centuries.

The Camera as Archaeologist

Photography, at its essence, is about seeing. But fine art photography asks us to see differently — to look at the familiar and find the extraordinary hidden within it. When I photograph decay, I'm performing a kind of visual archaeology, excavating beauty from what others might dismiss as ugly or worthless.

The Materia series was born from this impulse. I spent months photographing surfaces — walls, floors, metal, wood — all bearing the marks of time and use. Each image is a portrait, really. A portrait of time itself.

The crack in the wall is not a flaw. It's a map of forces, a record of movement, a beautiful scar that tells the truth about impermanence.

Technical Approach

For this kind of work, I prefer to shoot with natural light whenever possible. The quality of light matters enormously when you're trying to reveal texture. Harsh midday sun can flatten surfaces, while the raking light of early morning or late afternoon creates shadows that bring out every detail.

I typically work with a macro lens or a sharp prime, getting close enough to the subject that it becomes almost abstract. The goal is to remove the object from its context, so the viewer sees only the pattern, the texture, the color — the raw visual information stripped of its usual associations.

Finding Your Own Path

If there's one thing I've learned from this practice, it's that beauty is not a fixed destination. It's a way of looking. Train your eye to see beyond the surface, and you'll find that the world is far more visually rich than you ever imagined.

title: Between Presence and Absence
subtitle: Exploring liminal spaces in contemporary photography
excerpt: Liminal spaces — thresholds, corridors, empty rooms — hold a particular fascination for me. They are places of transition, pregnant with potential, existing between what was and what will be.
content:
The word 'liminal' comes from the Latin limen, meaning threshold. A liminal space is a transitional space — a place between places, a moment between moments. Think of a hallway, an empty parking lot at night, an airport terminal in the early hours of morning.

These spaces fascinate me because they exist in a state of suspension. They are designed for passage, not for staying. And yet, when you do pause in them — when you stop and really look — they reveal something profound about the human condition.

The Psychology of In-Between

There's a reason liminal spaces feel unsettling. They trigger a deep psychological response. We are creatures of context, and when context is stripped away — when a space is neither here nor there — we feel a kind of existential vertigo.

This is exactly what makes them such powerful photographic subjects. The discomfort they create is productive. It forces the viewer to confront their own relationship with space, with presence, with the passage of time.

The Liminal Spaces Series

My Liminal Spaces series began almost by accident. I was photographing in an old hospital that was being converted into apartments. The building was in that strange phase between its old life and its new one — emptied of furniture and medical equipment, but not yet filled with domestic life.

Walking through those corridors, I felt something I can only describe as the weight of absence. The space was physically empty, but it felt full — full of echoes, memories, the residual energy of all the human experiences that had taken place there.

A truly empty space is never really empty. It's full of the absence of everything that was once there.

That series taught me that photography doesn't need a traditional 'subject' to be compelling. Sometimes the most powerful thing you can photograph is nothing at all — or rather, the shape that nothing takes when it occupies a space.

title: On Seeing Slowly
subtitle: In a fast world, the deliberate eye finds more
excerpt: We live in an age of visual overload. Millions of images compete for our attention every day. My practice is a deliberate act of resistance — choosing to see slowly in a world that demands speed.
content:
The average person encounters somewhere between 4,000 and 10,000 images every single day. Advertisements, social media posts, news photos, memes — an endless torrent of visual information washing over us, each image competing for a fraction of a second of our attention.

In this environment, the act of looking carefully — of truly seeing — has become almost radical. It is an act of resistance against the tyranny of the scroll, the swipe, the endless feed.

The Practice of Attention

When I'm working on a new series, I begin not by picking up my camera, but by walking. I walk slowly through a space, looking at everything and photographing nothing. I let my eyes adjust. I wait for the light to speak to me, for a particular shadow to catch my attention, for a texture to reveal its story.

This might take minutes. It might take hours. Sometimes I leave without making a single exposure, knowing that the image I need isn't ready to be found yet.

Why It Matters

In a world that prizes speed and productivity, choosing to work slowly is not laziness. It's a form of respect — respect for the subject, for the medium, and for the eventual viewer of the work.

A photograph made in haste is often a photograph that looks like a thousand others. A photograph made with patience, with careful attention to light and composition and feeling, has a chance of showing us something we haven't seen before.

The camera sees everything, but the photographer must choose what to reveal. That choice is the art.

I encourage anyone who picks up a camera — whether professional or amateur — to practice this kind of slow seeing. Leave your phone in your pocket. Stand in one place for five minutes. Look up. Look down. Notice the way light falls differently on the same surface as the minutes pass. The world will reward your patience.
